stem: Two competitors license the same frontier model. Where does a lasting advantage come from, according to the FDE School?

options.a: Negotiating a lower price per token than the competitor
options.b: Switching each quarter to whichever model leads the benchmarks
options.c: Their ontology: a model of how their own operations run
options.d: Training a foundation model of their own from scratch

explanation: Frontier models converge and get cheaper, and anyone can rent them. The ontology captures your operations' facts and rules, belongs to you, and compounds with each use case.
author: claude-spec

stem: What is a hallucination in a large language model?

options.a: A fluent, confident answer that is factually wrong
options.b: A leak of the data the model was originally trained on
options.c: A refusal to answer a perfectly legitimate question
options.d: A slowdown caused by an overly long prompt

explanation: Fluency is not accuracy. Grounding the model in verified context reduces hallucinations; review where errors are expensive controls them.
author: claude-spec

stem: In the context versus cost-of-error matrix, where does 'build on your ontology' belong?

options.a: Little context needed, errors are cheap
options.b: Little context needed, errors are expensive
options.c: Deep operational context needed, errors are cheap
options.d: Deep operational context needed, errors are expensive

explanation: Scheduling, formulation, quality release and configuration need deep knowledge of your operations and punish mistakes. Generic tools fail there, which is why that is where margin sits.
author: claude-spec

stem: Most staff say AI makes them more productive, yet few companies attribute meaningful EBIT to it. What does the course see as the main reason?

options.a: Current models are still not capable enough for real business work
options.b: Freed time is rarely turned into decisions that change the P&L
options.c: Employees greatly overstate how much they actually use AI tools
options.d: Enterprise licences cost more than the time they save

explanation: Generic copilots save minutes for individuals. Money appears when AI targets the decisions that move margin and someone decides what to do with the freed capacity.
author: claude-spec

stem: Your team wants two months to choose 'the best model' before scoping any use case. What do you recommend?

options.a: Run the comparison first, because the model choice decides the outcome
options.b: Sign a three-year exclusive contract to lock in the best price
options.c: Start from the decision and its data, and design for swappable models
options.d: Wait for the next model generation before starting anything

explanation: Model choice is reversible and models leapfrog each other every few months. The decision, its euro value and the context the model needs are the hard, durable parts.
author: claude-spec

stem: Where does a small, inexpensive model usually belong in a production AI pipeline?

options.a: High-volume, narrow steps like routing or classification, proven by evals
options.b: The hardest multi-step reasoning step, where any cost saving matters most
options.c: Any step whose accuracy is not being measured yet
options.d: Nowhere: production should always run the largest model that is available

explanation: Match model size to task difficulty and volume. Small models handle narrow, frequent steps well when evals prove it; keep large models for the steps that need them.
author: claude-spec

stem: In plain terms, what does a large language model do when it writes an answer?

options.a: It looks up the answer in a database of verified facts
options.b: It searches the internet and copies the best matching page
options.c: It predicts likely next pieces of text, one token at a time
options.d: It applies fixed rules that engineers wrote for each type of question

explanation: A language model generates text by predicting likely continuations learned from very large datasets. It does not look facts up, which is why fluent answers can still be wrong.
author: claude

stem: Your purchasing team wants one AI model to summarize contracts, classify supplier emails and draft replies. Is that realistic?

options.a: No: each of these tasks needs its own model, trained from scratch
options.b: No: language models can draft text but cannot classify it
options.c: Only summarizing is mature enough; the rest needs another tool
options.d: Yes: one general model handles these language tasks, with checks

explanation: One general model can draft, summarize, classify, extract and translate. Its strength is language; its outputs still need checking where errors matter.
author: claude

stem: A manager asks a public chatbot for your plant's changeover rules and gets a detailed, confident answer. How should she treat it?

options.a: As a guess: the model never saw your plant's rules
options.b: As reliable, since the model learned from huge amounts of data
options.c: As reliable, because the answer is detailed and well structured
options.d: As reliable once a second chatbot gives the same answer

explanation: A model knows nothing about your company's specifics unless they are put in its context. A detailed answer about rules it never saw is a plausible guess, not knowledge.
author: claude

stem: A vendor says the next model generation will eliminate hallucinations. What is the course's view?

options.a: Right: each new generation removes most of the remaining errors
options.b: They are inherent; grounding reduces them and review controls them
options.c: Right, provided the company licenses the premium version of the model
options.d: They matter only for creative writing, not for business documents

explanation: Confident wrong answers are a property of the technology, not a bug the next release removes. Grounding in verified context reduces them; review where errors are expensive controls them.
author: claude

stem: Your team is impressed because the AI's reports read as if an expert wrote them. What does that say about their accuracy?

options.a: A lot: well-written answers are usually the correct ones
options.b: That the model was trained on your company's own records
options.c: That the reports are ready to go out without any review
options.d: Very little: fluency and accuracy are separate things

explanation: Fluency is not accuracy. A model writes equally well whether it is right or wrong, so quality of prose says nothing about quality of facts.
author: claude

stem: The cost of a given level of AI capability fell more than 280-fold in about two years. What follows for an executive?

options.a: Lock in a long contract now, before prices start rising again
options.b: Wait for prices to settle before starting any AI project at all
options.c: Treat models as rented; invest in your context and deployment
options.d: Train your own model, since outside models will lose their value

explanation: Capability converges across labs and gets cheaper fast, so the model is a rented, interchangeable input. Advantage moves to your context (ontology, data) and to deployment.
author: claude

stem: Three vendors pitch AI tools built on different leading models. What should weigh most in your choice?

options.a: How well each fits your data, process and deployment
options.b: Which vendor's model topped the public rankings this month
options.c: Which underlying model is the largest, measured in parameters
options.d: Which vendor offers the lowest price per query this quarter

explanation: Leading models converge and leapfrog each other, so rankings and size change quickly. What lasts is fit with your context and the quality of the deployment.
author: claude

stem: What does the course mean by an AI agent?

options.a: A chatbot that answers employees' questions about company policies
options.b: A model trained on company data that replaces a whole job role
options.c: A recommendation engine that ranks products for each customer on the website
options.d: A system that carries out multi-step tasks with tools, under supervision

explanation: An agent plans and executes several steps using tools, such as reading an order, checking capacity and drafting the supplier email, while people supervise.
author: claude

stem: The length of tasks AI agents complete on their own has been doubling roughly every seven months. What follows for your AI plans?

options.a: Agents will soon need no supervision, so plan to remove all reviews
options.b: Revisit often which tasks agents can take on, as their reach grows
options.c: The trend is about to stop, so plan around today's capabilities
options.d: Wait until agents can run whole processes before starting any project

explanation: The scope of what agents can do grows fast (METR), so the list of candidate tasks should be revisited regularly. Growth in reach does not remove the need for supervision.
author: claude

stem: Your AI rollout plan measures success by how many staff use the copilot each week. What is missing?

options.a: A larger number of licences spread across the company
options.b: A survey of how productive staff feel using the tool
options.c: A link to decisions that move margin, with euro targets
options.d: A training session for every employee in the first month

explanation: Usage and felt productivity are not P&L impact. Money appears when AI targets decisions that move margin and the gains are sized in euros.
author: claude

stem: Most enterprise AI pilots show no measurable P&L impact. What does the course see as the usual cause?

options.a: Deployment and missing context, not the model itself
options.b: The models are not yet capable enough for business work
options.c: Employees refuse to use AI tools in their daily work
options.d: Pilot budgets are too small to pay for the best models

explanation: In the MIT NANDA study, failure came mostly from how AI was deployed and from missing context. Better or pricier models do not fix a pilot that never reached real decisions.
author: claude

stem: Your board prefers building AI internally because it feels safer than a specialized partner. What does the evidence cited in the course suggest?

options.a: Internal builds succeed more often, because the team knows the business
options.b: The two approaches showed about the same rate of success
options.c: Internal builds fail less often but take longer to deliver
options.d: Projects run with specialized partners succeeded more often

explanation: In the MIT NANDA study, projects with specialized partners succeeded about twice as often as internal builds. Feeling safer is not the same as succeeding more.
author: claude

stem: Staff want help drafting routine emails and searching documents. Little company context is needed and errors are cheap. What fits?

options.a: Build a custom system on your ontology
options.b: Automate it fully behind strict guardrails
options.c: Buy an off-the-shelf tool such as a copilot
options.d: Hire a team to train a dedicated model

explanation: Little context and cheap errors is the buy-off-the-shelf box of the matrix. Building or training something custom there spends money where generic tools already work.
author: claude

stem: Matching supplier invoices to purchase orders needs little company context, but mistakes cost money. Where does it sit in the matrix?

options.a: Buy off the shelf
options.b: Automate with guardrails
options.c: Assist a person
options.d: Build on your ontology

explanation: Little context but expensive errors calls for automation with guardrails: rules and checks catch mistakes before they cost money. Deep context is not what makes it hard.
author: claude

stem: All of a company's AI pilots are email drafting and document search. What does the context × cost-of-error matrix suggest about this portfolio?

options.a: It sits where pilots are common but little money is made
options.b: It is well placed, since these tools are the easiest to scale
options.c: It carries too much risk, since errors there are expensive
options.d: It needs much more context data before these pilots can work

explanation: Most pilots sit in the cheap-error, little-context box; most money sits where deep context meets expensive errors, such as scheduling or quality release.
author: claude

stem: Analysis has become cheap. What does that change for a purchasing department, according to the course?

options.a: Supplier negotiations can be handed over entirely to the AI tool
options.b: Contracts can be summarized once and then filed away for good
options.c: Purchasing can drop its yearly audit and rely on monthly reports instead
options.d: Each purchase order can be checked against its contract, not a sample

explanation: Checks once rationed by labor can now run on every order. The change is coverage, not removing buyers or audits.
author: claude

stem: Your plant has always adapted its process to fit standard software. What has generative AI changed here?

options.a: Standard packages now adapt themselves to any process automatically
options.b: Processes matter less, since the AI now decides how work is done
options.c: Building and changing software got cheap, so tools can fit the process
options.d: Little: standard packages remain the only sensible option for plants

explanation: Software became cheap to build and change, so tools can be shaped around how the plant actually works instead of forcing the plant into the package.
author: claude

stem: A model solved a hard contract-analysis task in a demo. Your team assumes it will also handle simple unit conversions. What is the risk?

options.a: Capability is uneven; test easy tasks on your own cases too
options.b: None: a model that handles hard tasks will handle easy ones too
options.c: Unit conversions need a separate model built for arithmetic
options.d: It will work only if given much longer and more detailed instructions

explanation: The capability frontier is jagged: excellent at some hard tasks, unreliable at some easy ones. Only tests on your own cases tell you where it fails.
author: claude

stem: Before rolling out a model to read your plant's quality reports, what evidence should Noor ask for?

options.a: A vendor demo on well-prepared sample reports
options.b: Results on a sample of your own real reports
options.c: Strong published benchmark scores for the model
options.d: The model's own stated confidence in its answers

explanation: Performance is uneven across tasks, so only your own cases show what the model does on your documents. Demos and benchmarks use someone else's data.
author: claude

stem: Two models pre-trained on similar data differ sharply in tone and in how well they follow instructions. What explains most of the difference?

options.a: Differences in the size of the web archives used during pre-training
options.b: The programming language engineers used to write each model's code
options.c: Post-training, such as instruction tuning and learning from feedback
options.d: The type of hardware on which each model happens to be running

explanation: Pre-training gives a model its knowledge of language; post-training (instruction tuning, reinforcement learning from feedback) shapes how it behaves and follows instructions.
author: claude

stem: Your team wants a reasoning model for every step, including simple sorting of incoming emails. What is the trade-off?

options.a: Reasoning models are cheaper per answer, so use them everywhere
options.b: Reasoning models cannot sort text; they only solve math problems
options.c: No real trade-off: reasoning models are the better choice for every task
options.d: Better on multi-step problems, but slower and costlier on simple ones

explanation: Reasoning models spend extra computation before answering. That pays on multi-step problems and wastes time and money on simple ones.
author: claude

stem: Your quality team keeps most of its knowledge in scanned PDFs and drawings, not databases. Does that rule out generative AI?

options.a: Yes: everything must first be retyped into structured tables
options.b: No: multimodal models can read images, PDFs and drawings
options.c: Yes: language models can read only plain text typed into a chat window
options.d: No: scanned documents are now read with perfect accuracy

explanation: Multimodal models read images, PDFs and drawings, which makes shop-floor documents usable. They still make mistakes, so outputs need verification.
author: claude

stem: A multimodal model extracts dimensions from technical drawings. Its first ten results look right. What should you do next?

options.a: Verify it on a larger set of real drawings before relying on it
options.b: Deploy it, since ten correct results show that it works
options.c: Convert all drawings to text first, as models cannot read images
options.d: Replace the drawings in the PLM with the model's extracted values

explanation: Ten good results are an anecdote, not evidence. Multimodal extraction is useful but error-prone, so it must be checked on a representative set before anyone relies on it.
author: claude

stem: A vendor's demo on your sample data looked flawless. What does it prove about production?

options.a: That the tool is ready to scale to every site in the group
options.b: That integration with your ERP and plant systems will be straightforward
options.c: That your teams will adopt it without much training or support
options.d: Little: demos run on clean data, production on messy, changing data

explanation: A demo on clean data proves nothing about production, where data is dirty, systems must connect and people must change how they work.
author: claude

stem: Your pilot succeeded on a cleaned spreadsheet export. Alex wants to announce a rollout date to all sites. What should come first?

options.a: Announce the date now to create momentum across the sites
options.b: Test it on live, messy data with real integrations and users
options.c: Switch to a larger model so that the rollout cannot fail at scale
options.d: Ask the vendor to repeat the demo for each site manager

explanation: Success on a cleaned export is a demo effect. Live data, integrations and real users are where deployments fail, so prove the tool there before committing dates.
author: claude

stem: A manager expects agentic software to deploy faster than classic SaaS because it 'figures things out'. What does the course say?

options.a: It is faster, because agents learn and configure themselves on arrival
options.b: It is about the same, provided the model is a top performer
options.c: It is harder: it needs more context, integration and change
options.d: It is faster, provided the vendor supplies a ready-made demo first

explanation: Agentic software is harder to deploy than classic SaaS: it needs your context, connections to your systems and changes in how people work.
author: claude

stem: Gartner expects more than 40% of agentic AI projects to be cancelled by the end of 2027. What should a manager take from this?

options.a: Fund agents only with clear value, known costs and risk controls
options.b: Avoid agent projects altogether until the cancellation rate falls
options.c: Expect the cancellations to come mainly from weak underlying models
options.d: Launch many agent projects at once so that at least a few survive

explanation: Gartner names cost, unclear value and weak risk controls as the causes. Settling those before funding avoids joining the cancelled share.
author: claude

stem: A model you deployed six months ago is overtaken by a cheaper, better one, but your design makes switching costly. What was the mistake?

options.a: Not running a longer model comparison before choosing
options.b: Tying the system to one model instead of designing for swaps
options.c: Not waiting six months for the newer model before starting
options.d: Deploying AI before the model market had settled down

explanation: Models leapfrog each other, so no comparison picks a lasting winner. Designing so models can be swapped turns each new release into an option instead of a migration.
author: claude

stem: A client requires that production data never leaves its own data center. What does choosing an open-weight model hosted on site imply?

options.a: Costs mostly disappear, since open-weight models are free to download
options.b: Quality is sure to match or exceed the best closed models available
options.c: Data residency is met, but your team carries hosting and maintenance
options.d: Evals become unnecessary, since you control the weights yourself

explanation: Open weights give control and residency, at the price of running, patching and upgrading the model yourselves. Free weights are not a free system.
author: claude

stem: Sam compares a closed model through an API with an open-weight model on own servers for a low-volume internal tool. What often favors the API?

options.a: Stronger guarantees that data stays on company hardware
options.b: Full control over when the model version changes
options.c: Freedom to modify and fine-tune the model weights directly
options.d: Lower maintenance burden for a small team at low volume

explanation: At low volume, hosting and maintaining your own model costs more effort than it saves. Residency, version control and weight access are arguments for open weights, not for the API.
author: claude

stem: A new model tops a public leaderboard. Your extraction pipeline runs on another model. What should decide whether you switch?

options.a: Its score on your task-specific eval set, with cost and latency
options.b: Its leaderboard rank, which reflects overall ability across many tasks
options.c: Whether other companies in your sector have already switched
options.d: Whether its vendor advertises a larger context window

explanation: Leaderboards measure general tasks, not your extraction. Task-specific evals, weighed with cost and latency, tell you whether a switch helps.
author: claude

stem: Your eval set for invoice extraction holds 20 clean examples, and the model scores perfectly. What is the main weakness?

options.a: None: twenty clean cases are enough to check the main path
options.b: It lacks the messy and edge cases seen in production
options.c: It should be replaced by a public benchmark for extraction tasks
options.d: The model should grade its own outputs to avoid human bias

explanation: An eval set is only as good as its coverage of real inputs. Clean examples hide the scanned, partial and unusual invoices where production fails.
author: claude

stem: A classification step runs at high reasoning effort and is slow. Evals show the same accuracy at low effort. What do you do?

options.a: Keep high effort, since more thinking adds safety
options.b: Switch the step to the largest available model
options.c: Add a second model that checks every answer
options.d: Lower the reasoning effort for that step

explanation: Reasoning effort is a cost and latency lever. When evals show no accuracy loss, the extra thinking buys nothing for that step.
author: claude

stem: Every request to your agent repeats the same long system prompt and plant reference document. Which lever cuts cost and latency most directly?

options.a: Caching the repeated prompt prefix across requests
options.b: Moving to a larger model with a longer context window
options.c: Raising the temperature to shorten the answers
options.d: Splitting the reference document across many more requests

explanation: Caching reuses the processing of an identical prefix, so repeated long context stops being paid for in full on every call.
author: claude

stem: Each night you classify tens of thousands of maintenance notes, and nobody reads the results before morning. Which lever fits?

options.a: Real-time calls to the largest model for the best accuracy
options.b: A reasoning model at maximum effort for each single note
options.c: Batch processing at lower cost, accepting slower turnaround
options.d: Manual classification by planners to avoid model costs

explanation: When nobody needs the answer immediately, batching trades turnaround time for lower cost per item.
author: claude

stem: Your scheduling assistant calls a single model provider, which has an outage during the morning planning meeting. What design would have helped?

options.a: A longer timeout, waiting until the provider recovers
options.b: Retries with backoff and a fallback to another model or provider
options.c: Moving to the largest model offered by the same provider
options.d: A higher rate limit purchased from the same provider in advance

explanation: Providers have outages and rate limits. Retries handle short glitches; a fallback model or provider keeps the service running through a real outage.
author: claude
